title: What did you do yesterday? — the past tense
goal: Talk about what has already happened — and accept one fact that English never forces on you: the Bosnian past tense reveals the speaker's gender.
bekal: forming the perfect with *sam/si/je* + a form ending in *-o / -la / -li*
negating and asking in the past: *nisam radio*, *jesi li radio?*
stringing a short story together with *prvo, onda, poslije toga, na kraju*

notes: **Notice that Amina says *zvala sam* and *mislila sam*, while Budi says *bio sam* and *došao sam*.** The Bosnian past tense reveals the speaker's gender, and there's no way around it. English never makes you state this, so it may be the strangest thing in the whole course. The easiest way to get used to it: practice your own stories, in the form that fits you, until it comes out automatically.

***Nisam zaboravio* — the negative uses *nisam*, not *ne sam*.** The formula is exactly the same as for ordinary sentences, only the helping verb is swapped: *sam radio* → *nisam radio*. And questions use the long form: *Jesi li radio?* is answered *Jesam* or *Nisam*.

***Zašto se nisi javio?* — two little words in a row.** *Se* and *nisi* both compete for second place, and their order follows the table in Unit 12: helping verb first, then *se*. Here *zašto* takes first place.

***Emir je platio* — but *baterija mi se ispraznila*, without *je*.** In the third person singular, *je* is **dropped** when the sentence already has *se*. *On se vratio*, not *on se je vratio*. In all other forms the two live side by side: *ja sam se vratio*.

**Trebević.** The mountain south of Sarajevo, home to a cable car (*žičara*) built in 1959, destroyed in the war and reopened in 2018 — now a symbol of the city's recovery. On top still lies the bobsleigh track from the 1984 Winter Olympics, overgrown with moss and covered in graffiti. Go up toward late afternoon; from there the whole Sarajevo valley spreads out like a map.

grammars.title: The perfect — the formula
body: The only past tense you need at A1, and it does everything: "I worked yesterday", "I have worked", "I've ever worked". The formula has two parts: **the short form of the helping verb *biti* + the verb's *-o / -la* form**.
after: **The plural has two forms: *-li* and *-le*.** *-li* is used for groups of men **and** mixed groups — so one man among ten women is enough to change the whole sentence. *-le* only when everyone is female. (There's also *-la* for the neuter plural, but you'll hardly ever need it.)

**The helping verb is still a little word**, so it obeys the second-place rule: *Radio sam* (verb in front) or *Ja sam radio*, but **never** *Sam radio*. In the negative the order is actually freer, because *nisam* isn't a little word: *Nisam radio* can start a sentence.
**Asking:** *Jesi li radio?* or *Da li si radio?* Short answers use the long form: *Jesam* / *Nisam*. It's exactly the same pattern as in Unit 1, just with a verb added at the end.

**One tense, three meanings.** In the past, Bosnian doesn't distinguish "I worked", "I was working" and "I have worked" — they're all *radio sam*. If you need to stress that the work was finished, what changes is **the verb**, not the tense: *uradio sam*. That's *vid* (aspect), and it's the topic of the next unit.

grammars.title: Building the -o / -la form
body: Drop *-ti* from the dictionary form, then add the ending. Only about ten verbs need to be learned separately — and they're all verbs you use every day.
after: **The pattern: drop *-ti*, then add *-o* (m), *-la* (f), *-lo* (n), *-li / -le* (pl).** *Radi-ti → radi-o, radi-la.* Simple, and it works for most verbs.

**If the stem ends in a consonant, an *-a-* is slipped in before *-o*:** *rek- → rekao*, *mog- → mogao*, *doš- → došao*, *iš- → išao*. Note that the extra vowel appears **only** in the masculine form: *rekao* but *rekla*, *mogao* but *mogla*, *išao* but *išla*. This is the main source of confusion, and the only cure is to say both forms as a pair from the start.
**Verbs with *se* keep their *se*:** *vratio sam se*, *odmarala sam se*, *nismo se javili*. It stays in second place together with the helping verb.

**One habit that pays off:** every time you note down a new verb, write three forms, not one — the *ja* form (*radim*), the dictionary form (*raditi*) and the masculine past form (*radio*). From those three, every other form can be worked out without guessing.

blocks.text: Telling a story takes two things: time markers so the listener knows when, and linking words so the order is clear. Both are in this table, and you can use both as they are.

One four-sentence story using them all: *Jučer sam bio na Trebeviću. **Prvo** smo se vozili žičarom, **onda** smo šetali, **poslije toga** smo jeli pitu. **Na kraju** sam se vratio kući u osam, **ali** baterija mi se ispraznila, **zato** se nisam javio.* That's what A1 storytelling looks like — short, in order, and enough to keep a conversation going for five minutes.

blocks.title: Two other past tenses you'll see — and can ignore
items: The **aorist** (*rekoh, dođoh, bi*) and the **imperfect** (*bijah, govorah*) do exist in Bosnian, but they're almost entirely limited to literature, folk tales and old-fashioned storytelling. In everyday conversation, the perfect does everything.

The only truly living remnants of the aorist: ***bi*** in conditional sentences (*Da mogu, bih došao* — if I could, I would come) and ***rekoh***, which sometimes pops up as a storytelling flourish. Recognizing them is enough; you don't need to produce them until B1.
